The day's crypto news is a mixture of market positioning, fund flows, policy updates, and company decisions. The headlines below are worth reading for the detail behind them, not just the reaction on a price chart.

What is moving the conversation

Kalshi wants 24/7 Tesla and Nvidia perps as Wall Street fights over who regulates them. The prediction-market operator plans to seek U.S. approval for about 60 stock and ETF perps, taking one of crypto's biggest trading products into equities. Readers should check the original report before treating the headline as a confirmed change in the market.

India starts tokenizing $620 billion corporate bond market with digital rupee settlement. SEBI’s Demat 2.0 pilot turns corporate bonds into digital tokens and settles payment through the RBI’s wholesale digital rupee, with secondary trading and retail access expected in later phases. Readers should check the original report before treating the headline as a confirmed change in the market.

Bitcoin below $77,000, Zcash leads losses as traders bet on a Fed rate hike. Ninety-five of the CoinDesk 100 fell over the past 24 hours, and bitcoin has shed more than 5% on the week. Readers should check the original report before treating the headline as a confirmed change in the market.

Ripple puts AI agents inside its $1 billion corporate treasury bet. The software can monitor cash, risk and forecasts and suggest financial moves, but humans still have to approve every action. Readers should check the original report before treating the headline as a confirmed change in the market.

New Clarity Act text tweaks DeFi, credit union provisions, but road ahead for bill remains murky. The Clarity Act needs 60 votes when the Senate returns from its recess next week. Republicans circulated a fresh draft on Thursday ahead of the vote. Readers should check the original report before treating the headline as a confirmed change in the market.

Why a new SEC plan could ease a legal headache for tokenized securities. The SEC's new proposal to overhaul transfer-agent rules could eliminate duplicate offchain shareholder records, reducing reconciliation costs and legal uncertainty for tokenized securities. Readers should check the original report before treating the headline as a confirmed change in the market.

Market context

Bitcoin is around $77,133 with a -1.25% 24-hour move, while Ether is around $2,464.16 with a -0.29% move. Those figures are a snapshot, not a forecast. The useful question is whether the move is supported by spot demand, volume, and a clear change in the news.

When the market is quiet, leverage and liquidity can matter as much as direction. A small headline can move price quickly when traders are positioned too closely on one side.

What to watch next

  • New ETF creations and redemptions.
  • Futures open interest and funding rates.
  • Fresh regulatory text or official statements.
  • Security warnings, outages, or custody changes.
  • Whether the reported developments become live products rather than announcements.

The fairest reading today is cautious attention. There are real developments in the industry, but none should be stretched into a guaranteed market direction.

items.title: What are stablecoins, and how are they regulated? | Brookings
items.description: The European Union in 2023 adopted the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation, which sets requirements for the composition of reserves, prohibits charging fees for token redemption, and prohibits stablecoins from paying interest. In addition, it limits the daily non-investment transaction volume of any stablecoin not backed by a single European currency, citing risks “to financial stability, the smooth operation of payment systems, monetary policy transmission or monetary sovereignty.” [...] In July 2025, Congress passed the GENIUS Act, which establishes a federal regulatory framework for stablecoins. Similar to the U.S.’s dual banking system, stablecoin issuers may apply for approval from either federal or (if total issuance is below $10 billion) state regulators in states where such regulation exists. Issuers must back their stablecoins one-to-one with reserves of cash or other permitted assets—such as Treasury securities, repurchase and reverse repurchase agreements, government [...] be regulated by the applicable state or federal bank regulators. State and federal regulators have until July 2026 to finalize implementation rules, including stablecoins’ tax characterization, standards for foreign stablecoins sold in the U.S., and policies regarding conflicts of interest for stablecoin issuers, an issue of public debate given the Trump family’s growing business in crypto assets. items.title: Geopolitical Events and Crypto Price Moves
items.description:
In 2023, geopolitical instability due to the Israel-Hamas conflict raised concerns over potential oil supply disruptions. If such conflicts were to interfere with major energy routes like the Strait of Hormuz, this could increase oil prices, fueling inflation fears and prompting further central bank rate hikes. In such scenarios, crypto markets often experience volatility due to reduced liquidity and shifts in investor sentiment.

### SEC and regulatory actions [...] Demand for stablecoins like Tether surged as these digital assets provided an alternative to local fiat currencies under stress. Meanwhile, Bitcoin and other major coins saw increased demand as global investors speculated that digital assets might serve as a hedge against the economic fallout from the conflict, which affected energy and financial markets worldwide. [...] The U.S. Federal Reserve’s decisions on interest rates have been a primary driver for crypto market volatility in 2023. For instance, Bitcoin prices dropped following announcements of rate hikes, as higher interest rates often strengthen the dollar and attract capital to safer assets. When bond yields rose, many investors moved away from cryptocurrencies to avoid exposure to the higher risk and volatility of the crypto market.

Ethereum maintains its recent breakout

Bitcoin ETF inflows remain positive
